# Questions Men Ask {#feedback}

> "for a righteous man falls seven times and rises up again"
>
> — Proverbs 24:16

This book has no quarrel with the man in the trap. Its quarrel is with the trap. Every man who walks out is a cause for gladness. Two kinds of reader spoil it.

## The man who goes back in {-}

The first is the man who reads the final warning, gets free and finds it easy. A year later he is back where he started, and this time he half believes the method has failed him.

It's like pulling a man out of a flooded river. He lies on the bank coughing and thanking you. Six months later you walk past and he's wading in again.

When you're out, please don't be that man.

People assume he went back because he was still hooked and couldn't stand it. That's rarely true. Stopping was so easy that he lost his respect for the trap. He thought, "I could allow myself one now and then. If things go badly, I know how to get out again."

It doesn't work like that. Stopping is easy, and controlling it is impossible. The one thing you must do to be free of the habit is not do it. An easy door swings both ways.

## The man who won't jump, or jumps and struggles {-}

The second kind is too frightened to try, or tries and finds it hard going. His troubles come in four kinds.

### 1. Fear of failure {-}

Failing is no disgrace. Refusing to try is plain foolishness. Look at what you're protecting by not trying. You're protecting nothing. If you try and fail, you're exactly where you are today. If you don't try, you've failed already and saved yourself the trouble of hoping.

### 2. Fear of being miserable {-}

Ask the cold question: what terrible thing will happen to you if you never do this again? The answer is nothing. All the terrible things lie the other way.

The panic itself is part of what the habit did to you, and it passes. Being rid of that fear is the best thing you gain. If it rises, breathe slowly. If you're in company and people are grinding you down, step outside. Stand in the yard or the parking lot for five minutes.

And if you feel like crying, cry. Don't be ashamed of it. We teach boys to clench their jaws and swallow it, and it does them no good. King David wept, and so did Jesus. The clock is on your side. Every hour that passes, the Little Monster is weaker.

One serious word. What you feel may be darker than a bad day. If you find yourself thinking about harming yourself, put this book down and talk to someone today: a doctor, a pastor, a crisis line. The Appendix lists some. That isn't the Little Monster, and no book is the right tool for it.

And one more, said as gently as I know how. For some men this habit didn't begin with curiosity. It began after something was done to them as children. One therapist was abused himself. He says that most of the men who come to him were too, and that most have never told a soul. If that is part of your story, hear two things. What was done to you was not your sin. And telling someone who knows how to help, a counselor trained in trauma, is part of getting free. This book can clear away the lies about the habit, but it can't do that work for you. The Appendix says where to start.

### 3. Not following the instructions {-}

You'd be amazed. A man says the method didn't work for him, and then describes how he ignored nearly every instruction in it. He cut down, he kept the folder, he skipped the final step and he counted days. The instructions are gathered on one page in Chapter 32, so that nobody can say he wasn't told.

### 4. Misunderstanding the instructions {-}

These are the most common ones.

**"I can't stop thinking about it."**

Of course you can't, and you shouldn't try. Tell yourself not to think of a white horse and see what trots in. It's like chasing sleep: the harder you try, the wider awake you are. The effort is the problem.

It doesn't matter if the subject crosses your mind fifty times a day. What matters is *what* you think when it does. If you think, "I wish I could," or "When will this end?", you'll be miserable. If you think, "I'm free", you'll be glad fifty times a day.

**"When does the urge die?"**

Nobody can give you a date, and you don't need one. The leftover itch is so faint that you can't tell it from ordinary hunger, tiredness or a flat mood. That's why willpower quitters never know whether they've made it. Months later they feel hungry or low, and their mind says, "That's it again. You're owed one."

So don't wait for the urge to die. A man who waits keeps asking, "Is it gone yet? Am I really free if I still feel this?" and those questions produce the fear he was hoping would go away. If a twinge comes and you're a praying man, pray. One man wrote that whenever he does, he feels completely normal again. If you don't pray, say "I'm free" and get on with your day.

**"The moment when I know I'm free hasn't come."**

If you're waiting for it, you're building another phobia. What are you waiting for? You were free when you decided. The only job left is to be glad about it from the start.

**"I still want it."**

Then ask which part of you is speaking. A twinge is not a wish. The Little Monster wants feeding, and you don't want what comes after. But if you find you really do believe there is still something in it for you, then one of the old lies is still standing. That is no disgrace. Go back and find which one, and read that chapter again.

**"I feel as if I've stopped living."**

Why? Nobody asked you to. For a week or two you'll have a slight disturbance in the background: a faint, almost unnoticeable itch. Now think. You've had that itch for years, every hour you weren't feeding it. You had it at work, with your friends, at your mother's table and all night while you slept, and it never spoiled a meal. If you hadn't stopped, you'd have carried it to the grave.

The habit never added to a single occasion. It took from them. So go to the party and the wedding and the beach. Stay late and enjoy your dinner. Don't envy the smooth talker across the room with his three phone numbers. If he goes home alone to what you've left behind, he'd change places with you. You're not the one going without.

**"I'm miserable and irritable."**

Then something hasn't clicked yet, and that is no disgrace either. Some men understand every word of this book and believe it, and still set off like a man walking to the gallows. But you're doing the thing you most wanted to do, and what every man in the trap wishes he could do. Whatever method a man uses, the goal is a frame of mind in which every thought of the habit ends with "I'm free". If that's where you want to finish, why not begin there?

**"I fell. Am I back to zero?"**

No. There's no counter in this book, so there's no zero to go back to. Confess it today, refuse the second one, and find the lie that crept back. The short chapter after this one, If You Slip, takes you through it.

**"Should I tell my wife or my pastor?"**

Chapter 16 said secrecy is this habit's power and promised an answer here. You've already told God, and that matters most. If you're Catholic, that means Confession too. As for people, here's what I'd do.

*Tell one man.* A pastor or a priest, an elder, or an older friend with some sense. If you have nobody like that, a counselor or a doctor counts, and so does a helpline. If you're under eighteen, tell a parent, a school counselor or a doctor. The apostle James tells believers to confess to one another and pray for one another, and there's a reason. A thing that's been said out loud to another man loses half its size.

But be clear what you're asking him for. You're not hiring a policeman. A weekly "did you or didn't you" is the Willpower Method with a witness, and it keeps the subject at the center of your life. Tell him as a free man giving news: "This had me for years. It's over. I wanted one person to know." Then let him ask whenever he likes.

*Your wife.* A marriage is better with no locked rooms in it, so yes. Tell her, and don't leave it for years. She may already know, or half know.

Be clear what this is to her. To you it has felt like a private habit. To her it may be a betrayal, and she is entitled to call it that. So tell her for her sake. If you only want to unload your guilt so that *you* feel lighter, you're using her again.

Tell her once, and tell her the truth: what it was, for how long, and whether there was porn or another woman. Don't make her drag it out of you in pieces over six months. Half a confession followed by a second one does more harm than the first. Spare her the details unless she asks, and answer what she asks.

Then let her set the pace. She may be angry, or cold, or want to see your phone, or need time. None of that is a failure to forgive. Trust comes back slowly, and you don't get to say when. Don't ask her to keep score for you. But if she asks to look, show her.

Ask her what she needs, and mean it. If she wants a counselor, a pastor or a friend of her own to talk to, help her get one. If there was an affair, anything against the law, or anything that puts her health at risk, talk to a pastor or counselor first about how to tell her well. Do it soon.

She doesn't owe you praise for stopping. You owe her a husband who is all there. Chapter 31 has a section written to her.

*Nobody else needs to know.* Chapter 20 told you not to post "Day 1" anywhere, and that still stands. You don't need an audience.

## More questions {-}

**"My body doesn't work properly with my wife. How long until it does?"**

Chapter 8 described this. The honest answer is that nobody can give you a date. The medical student in that chapter was well in a little over a month. One recovery coach went through it himself. He says it was about two and a half months before things worked at all, and another six of gradual progress after that. A few men report longer. The sex therapist who has written most about it tells his patients, again and again, that the restraint he asks of them is "only temporary".

So be patient with your body, and tell your wife what is going on, because the worst part for her is thinking it's her fault. See a doctor too, since medicines and other conditions can cause the same trouble. And don't "test" things on your own in the meantime. You know what that is.

**"What about porn?"**

It goes with the rest, and not afterward or gradually. It's the same trap with a screen attached, and the two feed each other, as the man in the Introduction found out twice. Everything in this book applies to it. This book was inspired by [EasyPeasy](https://easypeasymethod.org/), which deals with porn alone.

**"What about sex?"**

This book has nothing against sex. It's against a counterfeit of it, and the counterfeit is everywhere.

Look at what we've all been sold. Porn teaches a man that women are for hire. The culture tells him he isn't a real man until he's slept with dozens of them. The same machine works on women from the other side. A phone full of likes teaches a girl that her body is what she has to offer, and that being looked at is the same as being loved. Men are taught to shop, and women are taught to put themselves on display. Both are lied to, and both come away emptier. We've been told this is freedom, and that it's normal. Look at the men and women it has produced, and ask yourself whether it looks like freedom.

The Bible's answer is old and simple: keep sex for marriage. The letter to the Hebrews, in the New Testament, says, "Let marriage be held in honor among all, and let the bed be undefiled". That isn't because sex is dirty. It's because sex is strong. It ties two people together, and lust wants the tie without the promise. Within marriage, sex is a gift, and Chapter 22 told the married man not to hold back from his wife.

If you've already lived the other way, this isn't here to pile on guilt. Nobody who wrote this book is an angel. Christians aren't the people who got it right. They're the people who finally admitted they couldn't, and asked for help. That's the heart of the whole faith. Look honestly and you find you aren't as good as you thought. Nobody is, and nobody gets there alone.

So if you're single, the answer is to wait. Don't go looking for somebody to use in place of your hand. That's the same lust, only now there's a victim. And if you're carrying a past, it's forgiven the same way as everything else in this book. You confess it, and you start again.
